newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Peaceful Bosnia poll highlights communal split.
newsitem.headline: Peaceful Bosnia poll highlights communal split.

text.p: Safet Kadic knew exactly what he wanted to do last Saturday -- go home and vote.

Sitting alongside a friend in a bus in a central Sarajevo depot, the smiling 70-year-old Moslem said he had no worries about returning to Rogatica from where Serbs had driven him out at the start of Bosnia's bitter war in 1992.
"They (the Serbs) can come over here, why can't we go over there," he said cheerfully.
His story was not typical. He and his friend were the only two people on the bus, and had a long wait until six other people boarded and it could leave with its required minimum load of eight.

Cocooned by NATO's 53,000-strong international police force, Saturday's first post-war poll passed off almost without violence, but underlined the country's deep communal divide and the lack of any real freedom of movement.

Across the country, some 20,000 out of a possible 150,000 made use of 19 guaranteed voters' routes to cast their ballots in their former home districts. About 4,000 Serbs came the opposite way, defying pressure to vote in the Serb entity.
They seemed out of step with the rest of the country.
With memories of mass expulsions, killings and rape still fresh, many opted to vote in special polling stations set up for "absentee voters" often only a short drive from their old homes.
International organisers were disappointed.
"I think many got cold feet at the last moment, others changed their minds when it was clear they would not see or be able to visit their old homes," said one U.N. official.
Analysts say the movement nevertheless involved the largest number of refugees returning to their home areas since the end of the war without large-scale harassment.
The international community says that limited movement offers hope for the future. Sceptics say it demonstrates the gap is now unbridgeable.

Throughout the election, the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) campaigned openly in favour of union with Serbia in defiance of the 1995 Dayton peace accords and poll organisers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Hardline Croats in their western fief, waving the national flag of Croatia, made little secret of their long-term hopes.

Even before the votes were counted and the results known, the country's nationalist parties signalled the start of a post-election power tussle. As during the campaign, there was little sign of a desire for reconciliation.

The Moslem Party for Democratic Action (SDA) said it would not accept the results in the Serb entity due to irregularities, earning a rebuke from international organisers who said it was not up to them to decide the poll's validity.
Under the Dayton accords which ended the war, the elections should lead the way to the creation of common institutions designed to reunify the country.
Diplomats say the SDA has begun manoeuvring to be able to reject a Bosnian Serb as the first leader of a three-man collective presidency made of one Serb, one Moslem, and one Croat.
Crucially, the candidate with the most votes becomes the first president or chairman of the rotating presidency and represents the country overseas.
Momcilo Krajisnik is virtually assured of winning the Serb seat on behalf of the ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party (SDS) and Bosnian President and SDA leader Alija Izetbegovic the Moslem seat.

Former Bosnian Prime Minister Haris Silajdzic, 50, is also standing and he could draw just enough votes from Izetbegovic to let Krajisnik emerge as overall winner and become the country's first post-war president.
"That result is unacceptable to the SDA, then you have gridlock, the international community is digging itself in here (Bosnia) whatever they say," said one U.N. official.
The international community, desperate to keep the momentum going, has lost little time trying to build on the positive aspects of the poll and move the Dayton process forward.
Paris and Bonn welcomed the poll even before it was endorsed by the OSCE and U.S. envoy, Richard Holbrooke, the main architect of Dayton, swung back into action.
After flying to Belgrade, Holbrooke announced Izetbegovic would meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, the real power behind the Bosnian Serbs, in Paris in three weeks time.
"We said we were going to launch an intense diplomatic effort (after the poll). This is the first manifestation of that effort," Holbrooke told reporters on Sunday.
